tagline.text: The national cemetery of fallen soldiers and presidents

location.label: Location
location.text: Bayani Road, Western Bicutan, Fort Bonifacio, Taguig

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (very crowded around All Saints' Day)

children.text: Located inside Fort Bonifacio in Taguig, this is the Philippines' national cemetery. War dead, soldiers and former presidents are buried here, and visitors can see the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and the war memorial pylons.

Libingan ng mga Bayani (Tagalog; "Cemetery of the Heroes" in English) is the Philippines' national cemetery, inside Fort Bonifacio in Taguig, Metro Manila. According to Wikipedia, it began in May 1947 as the Republic Memorial Cemetery, and President Ramon Magsaysay gave it its present name on October 27, 1954. A 1967 proclamation reserved about 142 hectares inside Fort Bonifacio for the cemetery.

It was first created to honor Filipino soldiers who fought in World War II, those who died in the 1941–42 Philippine Campaign and the 1944–45 Allied liberation of the Philippines. Burial eligibility later widened to include presidents, vice presidents, defense secretaries, chiefs of staff of the armed forces, senators, Supreme Court justices, veterans, National Artists and National Scientists. Presidents Elpidio Quirino, Carlos P. Garcia, Diosdado Macapagal, Ferdinand Marcos and Fidel Ramos are buried here.

It is closer to a place of remembrance than a tourist attraction. Walking from the Heroes Memorial Gate to the black stone walls with General MacArthur's words, then to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the center and the Korean War memorial pylon, gives you a quick sense of Philippine modern history. The Philippines fought in the Korean War as part of the UN forces, and its memorial stands here, which makes the site especially meaningful for Korean visitors. The cemetery is run by the Grave Service Unit of the Philippine Army Support Command. Because space ran short, annex plans began in 2007, and the only completed annex is a five-hectare site at Camp Hernandez in Dingle, Iloilo. In 2019 a five-year development program costing about ₱3.3 billion was approved, with the Bases Conversion and Development Authority reported to handle the first phase, so facilities may change; check the latest news before you visit.

The burial of former president Marcos remains a contested subject in Philippine society. He was buried on November 18, 2016 in a private ceremony with military honors, and protests took place in many parts of the country. When you visit, it is best not to bring up politics casually with locals.

This is the first structure you see on entering. A large concrete tripod has stairs up to a viewing deck and a metal sculpture at its center. It is the symbol of the cemetery and a popular photo spot.

Near the gate stand two black stone walls about 3.6 m (12 ft) high. They carry words attributed to General Douglas MacArthur in 1961, to the effect of "I do not know the dignity of his birth, but I do know the glory of his death."

The central monument of the cemetery honors Filipino soldiers whose names are unknown. The three marble pillars behind it stand for Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao. Wreath-laying ceremonies are held here during national events.

The Philippines joined the Korean War under the UN command. The memorial to the Philippine Expeditionary Forces to Korea (PEFTOK) stands in this cemetery, and many Korean travelers come specifically to see it. It sits alongside the memorial to Vietnam War veterans.
There is a memorial to Filipino guerrillas and one to the defenders of Bataan and Corregidor (erected in 1977). They show how Filipinos fought during the Japanese occupation.

A memorial also honors the soldiers and police officers who died in the 2017 Battle of Marawi in Mindanao. As it commemorates a recent battle, it reminds visitors that this history is still unfolding.

blocks.title: Graves of Presidents and Notable Figures

children.text: Former presidents Quirino, Garcia, Macapagal, Marcos and Ramos are buried here, along with figures such as former foreign secretary Carlos P. Romulo and former vice president Salvador Laurel. The grounds are large, so ask at the entrance or the administration office for directions to a particular grave.

The 142-hectare grounds have lawns and shade trees, a sharp contrast with the high-rises of BGC. Because the area is so big, many visitors move between the main monuments by vehicle rather than trying to walk it all.
Follow the guard's instructions at the main gate and arrive at the Heroes Memorial Gate. There is little shade, so going early keeps you cool.
Read the words on the black stone walls, then go to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and pause for a moment of silence.
Visit the Korean War memorial, then the Vietnam War, guerrilla, and Bataan and Corregidor memorials in turn.
Look for the grave of a president or notable figure you are interested in. Confirm the location at the local information desk.
Take a taxi or Grab toward BGC for lunch.
The grounds are large, so it is efficient to bring a car or keep a taxi waiting. On foot, moving between monuments alone takes a fair amount of time.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Combined with the Manila American Cemetery

children.text: See the main monuments of Libingan ng mga Bayani.
Move to the nearby Manila American Cemetery and see the other side of the same war.
Have lunch in BGC and finish with shopping or a stroll.
Both cemeteries are inside Fort Bonifacio, so they pair well in one day. Their opening hours differ, so check ahead.
By taxi or Grab from Ninoy Aquino International Airport, it takes about
40 minutes–1.5 hours
depending on traffic, and much longer at rush hour.
From Makati or BGC, a taxi or Grab takes about
15–30 minutes
. Enter "Libingan ng mga Bayani, Bayani Road, Taguig" as the destination.
Grab fares vary with time of day and demand.
According to Sakay.ph route listings, jeepney T227 (AFP/PNP Housing–Guadalupe via Bayani Road) passes the cemetery. The fare is listed at about
but may change, so check locally.
Combinations of MRT-3, bus and jeepney can also be searched on Sakay.ph by starting point.
The cemetery is large and walking between the main monuments takes time. Ask the entrance guard whether vehicles may enter and what the rules are.
If you take a taxi, tell the driver "Heroes Cemetery, Bayani Road"; most will understand. Check that the meter is on.
The dry season from November to May is comfortable for outdoor sightseeing. There is little shade, so go in the morning to avoid the midday heat.

Around All Saints' Day (Undas) on November 1, visitors flood in and it is extremely crowded. Reports said tens of thousands visited on All Saints' Day 2023, and hours were extended beyond the usual that day. Avoid this period if you want a quiet visit.

There are no hotels or restaurants inside the cemetery. BGC nearby has many hotels, restaurants and cafes, so it is easiest to handle lodging and meals there. There are also several Korean restaurants in BGC and Makati.
Eating and drinking inside the cemetery is not appropriate, so eat in BGC before or after and bring water in advance. Staying in the BGC or Makati area makes getting around easy.

A good plan is to see the cemetery in the morning and head to BGC around lunchtime. BGC High Street and the nearby malls have Filipino, Japanese and Korean food and cafes, so you can choose to taste. A meal ranges widely, from about ₱200 to ₱800.

Hotels and serviced residences in BGC are the most convenient. To save money, budget stays in Makati or Pasay are also reachable by taxi. Choose where to sleep the night before departure with the airport travel time in mind.

Check the opening hours and entry rules before you go. Guides differ on hours, so they are hard to confirm. See the information from the local administrator, the Grave Service Unit, or the Philippine Veterans Affairs Office.
Dress neatly and avoid sleeveless tops, short pants and slippers.
Since it is a military facility, carrying ID or a copy of your passport is the safe choice.
Ask at the entrance for the location of the Korean War memorial. It is the most meaningful spot for Korean visitors.
The grounds are large, so bring sun protection and water. Many stretches have little shade.
Combining it with the Manila American Cemetery on the same day makes the trip efficient.
Visiting presidential graves is politically sensitive. Check on site whether photos are allowed, and keep your distance during ceremonies.
Rather than a long standalone outing, it is easy to fit the cemetery into a morning slot of a BGC itinerary.
If you visit with family or children, explain the meaning of the monuments simply. The Korean War memorial is a good place to talk about the ties between the Philippines and Korea.
When calling a Grab, first confirm with the driver that the car can enter the cemetery, and it is easiest to call your return ride near the main gate.
This is a place of remembrance. Do not be loud or disturb ceremonies, and follow the guards' instructions since it is inside a military facility.
Photography may be restricted in a military area, so follow signs and the guards' instructions.
Access may be controlled during wreath-laying or burial ceremonies.
Around All Saints' Day there is extreme crowding and traffic control.
The grounds are wide with little shade, so watch for heat stroke on hot days.
The atmosphere can change on days with protests or political events, so check the news.
A cemetery for American war dead, also inside Fort Bonifacio, about
10 minutes
away by car. Seeing both shows two sides of the same war.
A new city district close to the cemetery with many restaurants and malls, good for meals and rest.
The financial district has many hotels and restaurants and is reachable by taxi.
If you want to learn more Philippine history, plan to visit the National Museum in central Manila as well.
